analysis.investment_thesis: Allied Blenders is dramatically overpriced by Magic Formula standards: Earnings Yield is only ~2.6% (EBIT INR 431 Cr / EV ~INR 16,867 Cr) while revenue has grown at just 3.3% CAGR over 5 years. Despite ROCE of 21.1% — the one positive — the valuation at 59.8x P/E negates any capital efficiency advantage entirely.
key_strengths: ROCE of 21.1% clears my 20% threshold — the underlying beverages business, anchored by the Officer's Choice brand, does earn reasonable returns on deployed capital
Operating Income surged from INR 243 Cr (FY24) to INR 431 Cr (FY25), suggesting genuine operational improvement, not just financial engineering
Finance costs declined from INR 173 Cr (FY24) to INR 126 Cr (FY25) as IPO proceeds repaid debt — balance sheet is cleaner post-listing
key_risks: Earnings Yield of ~2.6% is catastrophically low — I need >12% to even begin considering a stock; the market is pricing this as a high-growth compounder, which the 3.3% revenue CAGR does not support
Pre-IPO profitability was essentially zero: Net Profit was INR 1–3 Cr from FY22 to FY24; FY25's INR 195 Cr jump is the first real profit, raising questions about sustainability
OCF turned sharply negative in FY25 (INR -678 Cr vs +INR 186 Cr in FY24), and FCF collapsed to INR -806 Cr — the cash generation deteriorated exactly when the stock was priced for perfection
red_flags: P/E of 59.8x and EV/EBITDA of 33.4x for a company with 3.3% revenue CAGR — the valuation is irrational by any metric

Net Profit was INR 1–3 Cr for FY22/23/24; the FY25 jump to INR 195 Cr coincides with IPO equity infusion (equity tripled from INR 407 Cr to INR 1,558 Cr) — earnings quality and sustainability are unproven
OCF negative in FY25 (INR -678 Cr) despite reporting large accounting profit — cash conversion is deeply negative and unexplained
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Magic Formula computation: EBIT ≈ Operating Income INR 431 Cr (FY25). Enterprise Value = Market Cap INR 16,050 Cr + Debt INR 905 Cr − Cash INR 88 Cr = INR 16,867 Cr. Earnings Yield = 431/16,867 = 2.6%. This is less than a risk-free government bond yield — you are paying 38x EBIT for a slow-growing beverages company. While ROCE of 21.1% is the one bright spot (the Officer's Choice franchise does earn returns), the price paid for those returns is so excessive that the Magic Formula ranking would place this in the bottom decile on Earnings Yield.

The FY25 profit story deserves scrutiny. The company generated INR 1–3 Cr net profit for three consecutive years (FY22–FY24) despite EBITDA of INR 196–262 Cr — finance costs consumed everything. Post-IPO, debt was partially repaid and operating leverage kicked in with a 77% jump in operating income. However, OCF simultaneously turned to INR -678 Cr and FCF to INR -806 Cr in FY25, the opposite of what you'd expect from genuine operational improvement. This is a business whose listed equity is priced like a high-growth compounder despite delivering 3.3% revenue CAGR. A classic Magic Formula trap: decent ROCE, terrible Earnings Yield.
